cards.summary: 美国艺术与科学院下属项目Humanities Indicators最新报告显示，2025年美国高校共授予164,847个人文学科学士学位，为1991年以来最低，较2012年峰值下降30.4%。人文学科学位占全部本科学位的比例已从20年前的近15%降至8.1%。几乎所有人文学科分支的学位数量都在减少，其中宗教研究降幅最大。
cards.relevant: 人文学科萎缩反映了高等教育中STEM和职业导向专业的挤压效应，也折射出社会对文科价值认知的变化，对高校学科布局和人文教育未来走向有重要参考意义。
cards.context: 过去二十年，美国高校人文学科学位授予比例持续下降。2012年达到近期高峰后加速下滑，2021至2023年间降幅达12.7%。此后降幅逐年收窄，2024至2025年仅下降0.4%，为2012年以来最小年降幅，可能预示下滑趋势正在趋缓。

cards.source_text: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities。20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

cards.source_text: How Different Are Philosophers? (guest post) “Do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers?” That’s the question taken up by a team of researchers in a recent study published in Philosophical Psychology. Focusing on differences between philosophers and non-philosophers in regard to neurodivergent traits and responses to thought experiments, the researchers found some support, in the aggregate, for a “yes” answer to that question. The following guest post is by Thomas Nadelhoffer (College of Charleston), and is based on the article, “Thinking Differently: Neurodivergent Traits and Responses to Thought Experiments in Philosophers and the General Population,” co-authored with Paul McKee (Duke), Khaoula Boulhadi (Southern Connecticut State), and Helena Weymouth (College of Charleston). How Different Are Philosophers? by Thomas Nadelhoffer “The history of philosophy is to a great extent that of a certain clash of human temperaments [. . .] Yet, his temperament really gives him a stronger bias than any of his more strictly objective premises. It loads the evidence for him one way or the other” — William James Neurodiversity and Philosophical Intuitions In addition to being abstract thinkers, philosophers are stereotyped as being argumentative, overly self-absorbed in their own thoughts, and enjoy creating increasingly fine distinctions regarding everyday terms while imagining novel hypothetical situations and debating the conclusions they draw. It’s possible that many philosophers have quite distinctive personalities. More than two millennia before the modern notion of stereotypes existed, Plato used humor to poke fun at philosophers in the Theaetetus by telling a story of Thales contemplating the stars, so engrossed that he forgot where he was walking and fell down a well. However, do philosophers really think differently than non-philosophers? This was one of the questions behind the paper we recently published in Philosophical Psychology. We surveyed 1,254 individuals, 632 with formal training in philosophy and 622 members of the general public, and explored whether philosophers exhibit significant cognitive differences from non-philosophers using multiple measures of neurodiverse traits. To get enough responses from philosophers, we recruited participants here at Daily Nous and on Leiter Reports. We recruited the general population participants from Prolific. We preregistered our experimental design, research questions, and hypotheses. Phil

Their circumstances could hardly have been more different: one wrote his way out of scarcity; one was held under house arrest for a decade; one distilled an era’s medical knowledge into a text that ruled European universities for 500 years; and the last worked at the largest research institution of his age. But each shared the same underlying instinct: to move freely between mathematics, medicine, astronomy, philosophy and poetry, testing one discipline’s assumptions against another’s. My classroom is in Pakistan, where students arrive eager to talk about disruption and employability, but rarely about breadth. I want them to see, through these four lives, that this kind of expansiveness isn’t a luxury for stable times; it has produced some of the most enduring breakthroughs in the history of science. After 15 years working in liberal arts education, I believe a reintegration of disciplines in a Hellenistic style can lead the way. I’m not making a superficial case for ‘interdisciplinarity’. Instead, I’m arguing for something more specific: the recovery of the penchants of polymathy that once thrived in the Muslim world. Rather than fetishising disruptive innovation through compulsory courses on entrepreneurship and applied methods, we should offer an entirely different model of how to learn and what learning is for – especially since my students already enter university with a narrowly vocational mindset. The word polymathy itself captures the bricolage of many (poly) worlds of knowledge (mathy). Polymathy offers respite and reflection in a world fractured by war, climate catastrophe and injustice. Today, polymathy brings different kinds of thinking to bear on political, economic and environmental problems. cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.summary: Open Culture文章揭示，美国建筑大师Frank Lloyd Wright在建筑生涯之外，长期从事日本艺术品经销以补贴收入。文章探讨这段秘密副业如何影响了他的建筑美学，尤其是对日本空间观念和装饰元素的吸收。

cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. cards.source_text: In some rare cases, adaptations and interpretations of a literary work can surpass the source. Despite hundreds of valiant efforts on the part of fans, filmmakers, game/toy designers, and radio producers, this has never been true of the fully-realized fantasy world in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings trilogy (not that it’s ever been anyone’s intent). As we noted in a previous post, Tolkien’s fictional world is so intricate, its sources so vast and varied, that Corey Olsen, “The Tolkien Professor,” has made it his entire life’s work to open that world up to students and curious readers, such as with his eight-part lecture series on The Hobbit. One might also add illustrators to the list of Tolkien interpreters above who have—in the almost ninety years since The Hobbit’s publication and more than seventy years since the first appearance of The Lord of the Rings trilogy—done their best to visualize Tolkien’s world. But perhaps no one did so better than the master himself. Long known as a visual artist as well as a literary one, Tolkien left behind over 100 illustrations for The Hobbit, one of which adorns 2011’s HarperCollins 75th anniversary edition of the book. He also created these original cover designs for each book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy. In the long and complex publication history of Tolkien’s most famous of works, it’s unclear if these designs ever made it onto books published during his lifetime, but the sigil in the center of The Fellowship of the Ring design (above), with its ominous eye of Sauron surrounded by elvish runes and topped by the one ring, did grace the elegant, minimalist covers of the first edition of the trilogy. Tolkien’s artwork received a thorough treatment in a 1995 monograph J.R.R. Tolkien Artist & Illustrator, which covers over 60 years of Tolkien’s life as an artist, and the magic of flickr brings us this compendium of Tolkien illustrations. cards.source_text: Naomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be called New Gaza. The World Economic Forum get-together in Davos, Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave. At that same Davos, Donald Trump announced his Board of Peace for the reconstruction of Gaza – it has delivered nothing substantial in the seven months since, but more significantly, Klein says, “we’re being hit with so many extraordinary events that it’s hard to hold on to what a big deal it is: they have announced a privatised United Nations”. “I think we understand that wealth compounds, right? Certainly rich people understand that wealth compounds,” Klein continues, speaking to me from her peaceful, roomy study in British Columbia. “But I don’t feel like we spend a lot of time really thinking about the implications of what it means for that much wealth to be compounded, and what that does psychologically. Part of the new shamelessness we’re seeing is just what happens when this amount of financial, mediagenic, technological and military weaponry is concentrated in the hands of this very small, unaccountable group of people. They stop trying to seduce us in any way.” Klein looks calm and curious as she delivers this message. She has a ready laugh. cards.source_text: More than 500 people have invaded Brazil’s Ituna/Itatá Indigenous Land in recent weeks, opening illegal roads, setting deliberate fires and threatening federal agents. The area is home to the Igarapé Ipiaçava Indigenous people who live in voluntary isolation with no contact with outsiders. On Aug. 26, a federal court ordered the government to deploy the National Public Security Force within 48 hours to contain the invasion. As of Sept 11, the forces hadn’t yet arrived. The recent invasion followed the creation of the Bacajaí Environmental Protection Area (APA Bacajaí) under a new state law, which allows private landowners to build homes and raise livestock. However, APA Bacajaí completely overlaps the federally protected Indigenous land in Pará state, creating legal confusion that authorities say has been weaponized by land-grabbers to justify occupation for cattle ranching and other agricultural activities. The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office (MPF) has asked a federal court to fine the government 50,000 Brazilian reais (about $9,000) daily for failing to deploy enough security forces to contain the invasion. The area is currently under a temporary land-use restriction order to protect the isolated people living there. The government has argued it needs authorization from Pará’s government, which hasn’t cooperated. However, federal prosecutors say the federal government can be deployed on federal land without state authorization. Both the federal government and the state of Pará did not reply to Mongabay’s requests for comment by the time of publication. In its press statement, the MPF said the Indigenous Affairs Agency (Funai) and Federal Police overflights have detected the use of heavy machinery and chainsaws to clear more than 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) of forest trails and clandestine roads to mark illegal plots in the Indigenous land. Nghikembua said nearly all the able-bodied people of his village have left, leaving behind only the elderly, like himself, “Those who still had some strength left felt forced to leave the village for Namibia.” More than 1.8 million people live in Cunene and nearly 75% of the population is rural and depends on pastoralism and subsistence farming. “Southern Angola has experienced repeated severe droughts, extreme heat and environmental degradation for quite a number of years, leaving families without water, crops, or livestock,” said Victor Nyamori, an Amnesty International researcher and migration lawyer who collected the testimonies for the recently published report featuring Nghikembua. cards.source_text: In 1999 a journalist asked a then-unknown author to share her millennium wish. The author, who was 51 years old and had published only one book before, said she hoped her new one, out that year, would become a classic. “But then straight away I said: ‘Only joking!’ Because I didn’t want to sound full of myself, and I certainly didn’t think the wish would come true,” she remembers today. That author is Julia Donaldson; the book she published in 1999 was The Gruffalo; and, as you hardly need telling, her wish did indeed come true. And how. Since its publication, more than 18.2m copies of The Gruffalo and its sequel have sold worldwide. The Gruffalo’s Child was published in 2004, and together these tales of the terrible creature with terrible claws, and terrible teeth in his terrible jaws, have helped Donaldson to sell more than 50m books in the UK. In 2025 she was named the country’s bestselling author – across all genres, children’s and adult’s – since records began. Now the Gruffalo is making what Donaldson – who was made a dame in June – confirms will be his final outing. Gruffalo Granny, out this week, extends the protagonist’s family back a generation. In the new book, the Gruffalo and his daughter are awaiting a visit from Granny Gruffalo. The mouse, who played a pivotal role in the first and second books, is again centre stage; and longtime characters owl, fox and snake are all part of the action too. When we meet in a swish hotel in central London, I’m struck by the similarities between Donaldson and her new character. Her hair, like the Gruffalo Granny’s fur, is grey; in Donaldson’s case, it’s a neat bob, curled under at the ends. She is wearing a blue floral dress and navy shoes, and when she smiles her eyes twinkle; but I suspect that, like the Gruffalo Granny, she has prickles that reveal themselves when needed. What’s more, she has nine grandchildren, aged between five and 16. So is she the Gruffalo Granny? “Not really,” she says. “I’m the mouse.” The new book, she says, is a celebration of storytelling. “The mouse tells stories, then the Gruffalo’s child tells the stories to the granny, and the granny is going to read them back again. cards.source_text: Rewilding areas do not usually conform to traditional notions of beauty in England’s green and pleasant land. Detractors may bewail the beaver-felled trees, untidy scrub, deadwood, weeds, mud and “mess”. But a new exhibition highlights the aesthetic delights that can be discovered on rewilding sites where fungi grows on dying trees, water buffalo gather in new wetlands and brown-watered beaver pools flood once-desiccated fields. The artist Rebecca Howard devoted two years to visiting rewilding projects across England before spending a month painting each of nine large canvases that reveal what happens when people step back from intensive management of land and allow wild nature to take a leading role. “I wanted to create a positive exhibition that people could view and feel empowered to do something of their own, and not feel totally overwhelmed by the challenges we face with our climate and biodiversity crisis,” said Howard. “If you walk into an art gallery you’re faced with seascapes or bluebell woods but you don’t often see a dead tree in a painting.” Howard, whose exhibition opens at rewilded Knepp, West Sussex, on 12 September, began by visiting Cabilla, a fragment of Cornish temperate rainforest which is being restored and extended by the Thousand Year Trust charity founded by Merlin Hanbury-Tenison. But Howard was also invited into less widely known projects including, in Derby, the largest urban rewilding project in Britain, and Broughton Sanctuary, a North Yorkshire estate owned by the same family for more than 900 years that is taking a land-healing turn in the 21st century. Known as “P-22”, the number assigned by the team of biologists that first identified him, the lion gained national fame after photographer Steve Winter captured an iconic image of him prowling through Griffith Park with the Hollywood sign in the background. The sculpture, by Los Angeles artist Adam Matano, will be installed at the park’s visitor center, according to the National Wildlife Federation, which championed the project through its Safe LA Cougars campaign. Matano’s interest in how wild animals navigate the encroachment of our growing cities dates back to his teen years, he said. He grew up in Rhode Island, surrounded by empty lots. But by the time he reached his teen years, they had been developed into homes. “I love my favorite hiking spots,” Matano said. “But I kept thinking, ‘what happens to the animals?’” His sculpture shows a muscular P-22 stepping down from one podium to a second, more freeform and rocky pedestal. The rear podium contains a series of panels depicting local wildlife navigating the city environment – a mule deer crouching through a broken fence, a coyote ambling along against a backdrop of downtown LA, a raccoon and a gray fox in front of the Atwater bridge and the 5 freeway. “It’s about how you can’t contain nature,” Matano said. “Most people would think it woud be impossible for a mountain lion to live inside the city. But P-22 showed it is possible to co-exist. We should include nature when we design our cities.” He made a point of portraying P-22 with the GPS radio collar that enabled biologists to study him. “I think the radio collar is kind of misunderstood,” Matano said, noting that geolocation has become one of the most important tools available for understanding how wildlife moves across the landscape, offering insight into how to stitch portions of the fragmented natural world back together. “If we don’t want to see the collars, then we need to do better with our wildlife,” Matano said. “It’s really important that we understand where these animals are going and how they’re living.” Matano tried to capture the “idea of the wild entering Los Angeles and awakening the city to the nature already within it”, he said in a statement. cards.source_text: For several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompanying sense of mild anger. It was so easy to make us, the readers, angry – at the characters; at the author; perhaps even at the nature of this reality on which we’d lost our grip. We were confronted with the fact that our capacity to understand the world was limited. We didn’t like that. Irish author Adrian Duncan’s fifth novel, A Thought Without Collision, takes risks with this bafflement: it relates and conveys an experience of being mystified by the universe. As it opens, in Ireland in 1923, it is becoming apparent that six-year-old Catherine has exceptional academic gifts, and that her father’s farm is failing. In the next chapter, set in 1951, Dr Josef Alois, a Tyrolean émigré academic in his mid-50s, is living in his self-built house on the east coast of Scotland. He is alone until Catherine reappears, “a handsome woman in her mid-thirties”, and now an Oxford professor. The second chapter ends starkly: Alois “is more unwell than he believes and will perish in one month and eleven days”. Details of Alois’s biography, and aspects of his two books, are drawn from the life of Ludwig Wittgenstein. The novel references the philosopher’s near-contemporaries, GE Moore, Gottlob Frege and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Like Alois and Catherine, these men laboured to establish a particular understanding of the world. Some pages of A Thought Without Collision present diagrams or passages of algebraic logic. Throughout, descriptions of small, mysterious places (“pockets” in Catherine’s mind, pits dug in the ground, golf holes, a swallow’s nest) are emblems of the other worlds that surround us, intimated but not available to human knowledge. As Catherine’s intelligence becomes increasingly polymathic, her interest ranges from complex mathematics to animal sentience. She pictures hidden worlds in the sky: a “plane of translucent and unconnected fragments above them all”. The narrative is related in short, alternating chapters that switch between the two time periods. This creates a sense of flickering movement, like chevrons on a motorway: we see Catherine’s life speed by, an effect intensified by Alois’s impending death. cards.source_text: On a cloudy Spring morning, a group of 20 nature enthusiasts gather at the entrance to a nature park on the northern edge of Sydney. “Good to see nobody is wearing thongs,” our volunteer tour leader, Helen Logie, says to chuckles. We are among just under 5,000 people lucky enough to visit Muogamarra nature reserve during the six weeks a year it is open to the public, coinciding with wildflower season. This year, tickets – which provide access to a limited number of guided and self-directed walks – sold out in less than a week. On the windy drive in, cars slowed to marvel at waratahs, now in full bloom – one of the threatened species that people flock here year after year to witness. The fully native nature reserve, encompassing 2,300 hectares on the edge of the Hawkesbury River, has been protected for almost a century and inhabited by traditional owners for at least 20,000 years. Its fragile ecosystem and Aboriginal cultural heritage cuts it off to public access for most of the year, providing a unique experience. The park was a prominent Aboriginal meeting place and is littered with shell middens and sacred sites, some of which remain inaccessible to the public. In the 1930s, the conservationist and engineer John Duncan Tipper took a lease of about 800 hectares of the land. Tipper was concerned about continuing damage to Sydney’s national parks in what was a period of great species collapse in Australia. Koalas were being shot by the thousands, and great swathes of wildflowers were being cut down and sold in the city. We are heading out on two walks this morning, including Tipper Loop and a 2km trek to the western lookout. There are 900 plant species here, 14 mammals and more than 100 varieties of birds, but it’s the wildflowers that are the drawcard. Logie points out a huge Gymea lily, which producers clusters of trumpet-shaped red flowers, and smoke bush, which has intricate white flowers that – viewed close up – look like lace. As we inspect a woody pear, the sound of a fan-tailed cuckoo rings out in the distance. The trees here are hundreds of years old, the perfect habitat for native avian life. Logie says sometimes they spot wedge-tailed eagles and lyrebirds. There are even rumours of koalas – though nobody sees one. The soil here is sandstone, common to the steep ridge tops of the Hawkesbury, and volcanic. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 29 minute listen Early one morning in the late 12th century, Bishop Hugh of Lincoln arrived in the Hertfordshire village of Cheshunt. There, he was immediately surrounded by a crowd of people, who begged him to help one of their neighbours. And so, dismounting from his horse, he went to the man’s house, where he was confronted by the disturbing sight of a possessed man ‘lying prostrate with his head tied to a post and each of his hands to great stakes fixed in the ground.’ Despite these restraints, the man constantly writhed around, rolling his eyes, gnashing his teeth, and sticking his tongue out. To Hugh, as to the local onlookers, the diagnosis was clear: this unfortunate sailor had been possessed by a demon and could be cured only by an exorcism. Once the necessary rituals were performed, he was ‘delivered from the demon [and] … after living devoutly for some years, finally made a good and peaceful end.’ For Hugh’s biographer, Adam of Eynsham, the incident was worth recounting because it demonstrated not only that the future saint had healing powers, but that he was a brave and compassionate man (in sharp contrast to the local bishop, who had ‘galloped away as if pursued by the Furies’, rather than face a possessed man). But, to us, the story – full of fear, cruelty and superstition – sums up both everything that was wrong with medieval attitudes to mental illness, and the apparent uselessness of medieval medicine in the face of serious illness. And yet, as is so often the case when studying the distant past, the reality was rather more complicated. Influenced by stories of demonic possession (and there are lots of them, especially in saints’ lives and miracle collections), I long assumed that our ancestors’ attitudes to, and experiences of, mental health were completely different to our own – and that they would have little sympathy with our fast-growing mental health crisis. But when I turned my attention away from religious texts, and began to research medieval ideas about healthy living, I soon came across medieval people who discussed mental health in ways that felt far more familiar to me. The similarities were particularly apparent in medical writings, which outline a sophisticated argument that mental wellness was at the heart of a healthy lifestyle. cards.source_text: Georgia’s Fulton County D.A. Fani Willis spent over two years trying and failing to conflate YSL (Young Stoner Life) Records with a street gang. Willis, who cut her teeth wielding the state’s racketeering laws to prosecute schoolteachers, claimed (often through the use of lyrics, social media captions, and tattoos) that YSL was a front for “Young Slime Life,” a gang associated with the Bloods. She alleged a violent conspiracy that indicted 28 co-defendants, including YSL artists Gunna, Yak Gotti, and Duke, along with label head Young Thug, but failed to win convictions on the most serious charges. Still, Willis claims an “amazing” job done—an understandable position if you consider the stipulations of Thug’s freedom: 15 years of probation, a 10-year ban from Atlanta city limits, and a tarnished brand. cards.source_text: “I never actually wanted to be a DJ,” Simon Green, better known as versatile electronic producer Bonobo, recently told Mixmag. “It just kind of happened by accident.” Now, after 26 years spent exploring the nuances of downtempo and house music, he wants off the album-tour hamster wheel. Distance in Static is likely his last Bonobo album, he says—at least “in a traditional sense.” The British musician recently moved from Southern California to Japan and is eyeing film scores, art installations, and modular string quartets with Miguel Atwood-Ferguson as potential next steps. But for all his ostensible desire to stretch, he retreads familiar ground on Distance in Static. Bonobo’s eighth album is his clubbiest album yet, a reflection of the sounds and textures that have shaped his evolution from downtempo mood-setter to headlining dance act. More victory lap than self-contained artist statement, it completes a trio of records—following his last two full-lengths, Migration and Fragments—that get progressively heavier in sound but lighter in ideas. No score yet, be the first to add. Migration had, among many things, good timing on its side; released in 2017, it coincided with the post-EDM rush to reimagine what contemporary dance floors could sound like, and Green’s sensual, club-lite soundscapes perfectly met the moment—funky synths and devotional vocals drizzled over variations of UK bass music, often backed by live bands and full string sections. But that chill-adjacent formula doesn’t sparkle like it used to, and Distance in Static feels recycled, lacking the freshness and exploratory spirit that made Green’s earlier work interesting. While Black Sands-era Bonobo was intriguingly hard to categorize—glitchy, funky, jazzy, and dubby, too heavy for “chill” and too heady for “club”—Distance in Static sounds as if each track was engineered to suit specific environments or playlists. There are groovy R&B-soul excursions like the Joy Crookes team-up “Always on Your Side,” sleek cosmic interludes like “ID700” and “Uncasually,” and billowing, eyes-closed, stadium-rave cuts like “Drift” and “Cycles,” which echo each other’s mournful, heartstring-tugging synths. Despite Green’s determination to play in multiple sandboxes, the tidily siloed nature of these tracks also makes them feel more anonymous. “Me and You,” the project’s catchy lead single, should be a slam dunk—it’s bouncy, playful, tightly edited, and samples a 1950 Malawian field recording by ethnomusicologist

items.title: Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
items.summary: 20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities. As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%. These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Here are the numbers: In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012. And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline: Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs). How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase: In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918. The full report from Humanities Indicators is here. The post Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities first appeared on Daily Nous .

The author, who was 51 years old and had published only one book before, said she hoped her new one, out that year, would become a classic. “But then straight away I said: ‘Only joking!’ Because I didn’t want to sound full of myself, and I certainly didn’t think the wish would come true,” she remembers today. That author is Julia Donaldson; the book she published in 1999 was The Gruffalo; and, as you hardly need telling, her wish did indeed come true. And how. Since its publication, more than 18.2m copies of The Gruffalo and its sequel have sold worldwide. The Gruffalo’s Child was published in 2004, and together these tales of the terrible creature with terrible claws, and terrible teeth in his terrible jaws, have helped Donaldson to sell more than 50m books in the UK. items.title: A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonder
items.summary: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditions For several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompanying sense of mild anger. It was so easy to make us, the readers, angry – at the characters; at the author; perhaps even at the nature of this reality on which we’d lost our grip. We were confronted with the fact that our capacity to understand the world was limited. We didn’t like that. Irish author Adrian Duncan’s fifth novel, A Thought Without Collision, takes risks with this bafflement: it relates and conveys an experience of being mystified by the universe. As it opens, in Ireland in 1923, it is becoming apparent that six-year-old Catherine has exceptional academic gifts, and that her father’s farm is failing. In the next chapter, set in 1951, Dr Josef Alois, a Tyrolean émigré academic in his mid-50s, is living in his self-built house on the east coast of Scotland. He is alone until Catherine reappears, “a handsome woman in her mid-thirties”, and now an Oxford professor. The second chapter ends starkly: Alois “is more unwell than he believes and will perish in one month and eleven days”. Continue reading...
